title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: The Rostovs remained in Moscow until September 1 — the eve of the enemy's entry into the city.

After Petya had joined Obolensky's Cossack regiment and left for Belaya Tserkov where the regiment was forming, the countess was seized with terror. The thought that both her sons were at war — that both had left the safety of her wing, and that today or tomorrow either or both might be killed, as the three sons of one of her acquaintances had been — struck her that summer for the first time with cruel clarity. She tried to get Nicholas sent home and wanted to go herself to fetch Petya, or to get him assigned somewhere in Petersburg, but neither proved possible. Petya couldn't return unless his regiment did, or unless he was transferred to another active unit. Nicholas was somewhere with the army and hadn't written since his last letter, which gave a detailed account of his meeting with Princess Mary. The countess couldn't sleep at night, and when she did she dreamed of her sons lying dead. After many consultations, the count devised a way to calm her: he got Petya transferred from Obolensky's regiment to Bezukhov's, which was training near Moscow. Though Petya would remain in service, this transfer gave the countess the consolation of having at least one son within reach, and she hoped to arrange things so he'd never be sent to battle again. As long as only Nicholas was in danger, the countess imagined she loved her firstborn more than all her other children and even reproached herself for it; but when her youngest — the scapegrace who'd been bad at lessons, always breaking things and annoying everyone, that snub-nosed Petya with his cheerful black eyes and fresh rosy cheeks where soft fuzz was just beginning to show — when he was thrown among those big, terrible, cruel men who were fighting somewhere about something and apparently enjoying it, then his mother felt she loved him more, much more, than all the rest. The nearer the time came for Petya to return, the more anxious the countess grew. She began to think she would never live to see such happiness. The presence of Sonya, of beloved Natasha, or even of her husband irritated her. "What do I need them for? I need no one but Petya," she thought.

At the end of August the Rostovs received another letter from Nicholas. He wrote from the province of Voronezh, where he'd been sent to procure horses, but the letter did not ease the countess. Knowing one son was out of danger only made her more anxious about Petya.

Although by the twentieth of August nearly all the Rostovs' acquaintances had left Moscow, and everyone urged the countess to leave as quickly as possible, she refused to hear of going before her treasure — her adored Petya — returned. On August 28 he arrived. The passionate tenderness with which his mother received him displeased the sixteen-year-old officer. Though she hid from him her plan to keep him close, Petya guessed her intentions and, instinctively fearing that he might give in to emotion with her — might "go soft," as he put it to himself — he treated her coolly, avoided her, and during his stay in Moscow attached himself exclusively to Natasha, for whom he had always had an especially brotherly, almost lover-like tenderness.

Due to the count's habitual carelessness, nothing was ready for departure by August 28, and the carts that were supposed to come from their Ryazan and Moscow estates to carry away their belongings didn't arrive until the thirtieth.

From the twenty-eighth to the thirty-first, all Moscow was in an uproar. Every day thousands of men wounded at Borodino were brought in through the Dorogomilov gate and taken to various parts of the city, and thousands of carts carried residents and their possessions out through the other gates. Despite Rostopchin's broadsheets — or because of them, or independently of them — the wildest and most contradictory rumors circulated. Some said no one would be allowed to leave; others said all the icons had been removed from the churches and everyone would be ordered to go. Some claimed another battle after Borodino had routed the French, while others insisted the Russian army had been destroyed. Some talked about the Moscow militia marching to the Three Hills led by the clergy; others whispered that Father Augustin had been forbidden to leave, that traitors had been caught, that peasants were rioting and robbing people on the roads out of Moscow, and so on. But all this was only talk; in reality — though the Council of Fili, at which it was decided to abandon Moscow, had not yet been held — both those who left and those who stayed felt, though they didn't show it, that Moscow would certainly be given up and that they should get away as quickly as possible. Everyone sensed that everything would suddenly collapse and change, but through September 1 nothing had. Like a condemned man being led to execution who looks around and straightens the crooked cap on his head, Moscow involuntarily continued its usual life, though it knew the time of its destruction was near — when the conditions its people were accustomed to would be completely overturned.

During the three days before the occupation, the entire Rostov family was absorbed in various activities. The head of the family, Count Ilya Rostov, drove about the city constantly, collecting rumors from all sides and issuing hasty, confused orders at home about preparations for departure.

The countess watched the packing, was dissatisfied with everything, was constantly chasing after Petya — who kept running away from her — and was jealous of Natasha, with whom he spent all his time. Sonya alone handled the practical side, getting things packed. But lately Sonya had been particularly sad and quiet. Nicholas's letter, in which he mentioned Princess Mary, had prompted joyful comments from the countess — made in Sonya's presence — about seeing Providence at work in bringing the princess and Nicholas together.

"I was never pleased about Bolkonsky's engagement to Natasha," said the countess, "but I always wanted Nicholas to marry the princess, and had a feeling it would happen. What a good match it would be!"

Sonya felt this was true — that the only way to restore the Rostov family's finances was for Nicholas to marry a wealthy woman, and that the princess was an excellent match. It was very bitter for her. But despite her grief — or perhaps because of it — she took on all the difficult work of organizing the packing and was busy all day long. The count and countess turned to her whenever orders needed giving. Petya and Natasha, by contrast, were generally a nuisance and a hindrance. Nearly all day the house rang with their running feet, their shouts, and their spontaneous laughter. They laughed and were joyful not because there was any reason to be, but because gladness and mirth filled their hearts and so everything that happened gave them cause for laughter. Petya was in high spirits because having left home a boy he had returned — as everyone told him — a fine young man; because he was at home; because he'd left Belaya Tserkov where there was no hope of seeing battle anytime soon and had come to Moscow where there would be fighting any day; and chiefly because Natasha, whose lead he always followed, was in high spirits. Natasha was gay because she had been sad too long and now nothing reminded her of the cause of her sadness, and because she was feeling well. She was also happy because she had someone to adore her — the adoration of others was the lubricant her machinery needed to run smoothly, and Petya adored her. Above all, they were gay because there was a war near Moscow, there would be fighting at the city gates, weapons were being handed out, everyone was escaping and going somewhere, and in general something extraordinary was happening — and that is always exciting, especially to the young.
